title: Who Will Your Teenager Be?
author: Michael Perrone
summary: Michael Perrone argues that modern parents, facing an uncertain future and wary of imposing their own ideals, hand teenage formation to mass society and settle for hoping their children are happy, producing young adults who look grown but cannot thrive as adults. He says family culture has been reduced to the vibe of the home, so that the teenager becomes a consumer or even the customer of the family, and customers leave when they grow up. His alternative is to put teenagers on the family org chart as real owners, with duties whose failure has visible consequences, such as a "VP of Wednesday night dinner" or a "VP of Finance" who pays real bills. Since teens will never again have less responsibility than now, the future behaviour parents want, from church service to tidy rooms to responsible technology use, must be practised today. Perrone adds the harder condition that parents must embody what they ask, as limiting his own smartphone use was the price of limiting his children's.
points: Giving teenagers "space" and low expectations leaves them as customers of the family and unprepared for adult responsibility.
Real family roles with real consequences, such as paying bills and caring for siblings, turn adolescence into formation rather than waiting.
Each hoped-for adult behaviour needs a matching present-day mechanism, which is a family culture that puts its stated values on the calendar.
Parents must hold themselves to the standard they set; Perrone could not limit his teens' phones without first limiting his own.
The goal is a teenager who becomes a better version of the parent, not a product of peers or generational catchphrases.
quotes: The uncertainty that families face is also an underrated cause of the destruction of family and local culture: if teenagers have choices is not any inculcation, any imposition of family culture, any kind of family-rooted expectation akin to a straitjacket? Just a topic for a future therapist to unpack?

However, the result we see throughout society is a young man or young woman who looks like an adult but is incapable of thriving as one. A youth free to pursue their potential, but is stuck scrolling TikTok.
But what happens when the customer grows up? They leave. They aren’t interested in the “product” anymore except as nostalgia.
Being on the org chart allows teens to live by a set of adult expectations and standards, rescuing them from the neglect of low expectations.

This goes against the modern instinct, but at no future point in your teenager’s life will they have less responsibility, less social expectation, and less complexity to deal with than they do right now as a teen.
If my “VP of Wednesday night dinner” falters, then we have to eat leftovers or string cheese sandwiches.
It turns out to be far easier to limit a teenager’s screen time than to limit your own. And I couldn’t credibly do the former without first ruthlessly doing the latter.

The project of your family and mine is the formation of teenagers into capable adults; and specifically converting their character, choices and actions beyond the age of 18 into an extension of your family identity.
